name: Looksflation

card.summary: Community term for the idea that the attractiveness needed to earn a given rating keeps rising, which shapes how people set their own looks goals.
card.note: A forum theory about rating scales, not a measured phenomenon.

quick.overview:
Looksflation (also looks inflation) is looksmaxxing slang for the belief that standards of attractiveness drift upward over time, so a face once seen as very good-looking is now rated as merely above average on forum scales such as the PSL or tier system.

Members use the idea to explain why ratings feel harsher than in past decades and to calibrate their own goals: if the bar for "Chad" or "high-tier normie" rises, improving skin, grooming, body and facial presentation matters more to stay at the same relative level. The claim is discussed in forum threads; no formal study of rating-scale inflation was found.
quick.how: In practice the term is used as a lens when rating photos, comparing present-day men with older celebrities, and deciding which looks improvements to prioritise. It is a way of talking about standards rather than a product or procedure.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Forum posters themselves note that comparing against heavily filtered or edited images, and rating peers harshly, can affect confidence and how people treat one another.

lead: Looksflation, also written "looks inflation", is a term used on looksmax.org and related communities for the idea that the level of attractiveness required to earn a particular rating rises over time. It is borrowed from the economic word for a general rise in prices: the same face is said to "buy" a lower rating than it once did. Users apply it to the PSL scale and to tier labels such as HTN (high-tier normie) and Chad.[1][2]

It helps looksmaxxers by framing a goal. If standards are seen as rising, members argue that skin, grooming, leanness and styling are ongoing work rather than a one-off fix, and that rating inflation can make self-assessment inaccurate. Several threads use the idea to calibrate expectations, for example by asking who would still count as a top-tier face today.[1][2][3]

The term sits inside the wider rating culture described in encyclopedic coverage of looksmaxxing, where the PSL scale and tier labels are the shared vocabulary for judging faces.[9] The looksflation threads themselves are anecdotal, and no academic study of rating-scale inflation in these communities has been identified. Psychology does describe related effects, such as contrast effects in judging attractiveness and the halo effect, which some readers use to think about the idea, though those studies do not address looksmaxxing rating scales.[10][11]

chain: Notice that rating scales may drift upward
Compare self against realistic, not filtered, benchmarks
Prioritise visible improvements such as skin, grooming and physique
angle.text: Looksflation is a calibration idea. People who hold it use it to set looks goals against a rising bar, and to question inflated self-ratings or edited comparison images.

infobox: Filtered social media images, generous self-ratings, mainstreaming of rating culture

paras: Users describe looksflation as a ratcheting of standards: faces rated highly in the past are said to receive middling ratings today. One poster argues that actors from classic films such as Harrison Ford and Mark Hamill would now be rated around HTN on the forum, while conceding that Ford looked better in motion than in stills.[3]

A second strand concerns self-rating. A poster argues that average users rating themselves generously raised the perceived boundaries of tiers, so that more people are labelled high-tier than the scale originally implied.[2] A third strand concerns individual celebrities: in one thread a poster says half the forum would now rate a well-known model HTN, and a reply answers that his broad appeal places him alongside Chads regardless of the label.[1]

Looksflation is only meaningful relative to a scale. Encyclopedic coverage describes the PSL scale as running roughly from 1 to 8 and as intended to reflect how women perceive men, with tier names ranging from sub-3 through low-, mid- and high-tier normie to Chadlite, Chad and beyond.[9] Critics quoted in that coverage regard the scale as pseudoscientific, while participants treat it as a shared shorthand.[9]

Because the labels are informal and set by whoever is rating, members describe the boundaries between tiers as movable. That movability is the premise of the looksflation argument: if the boundary of a tier shifts, the same face moves between tiers without changing.[2]

Posters point to constant exposure to filtered, makeup-assisted and flatteringly angled images on social media as raising the benchmark for both men and women. One thread adds that this exposure is said to begin around age ten and to make typical partners seem less appealing by comparison.[3] A separate thread is titled around social media and looks inflation, treating the platform as the main driver.[5]

Others attribute it to the mainstreaming of looksmaxxing and rating culture, and to inflated self-ratings among users. In one thread the poster ties the change to the period around 2023, when rating talk spread beyond the original forums, and complains that generous self-ratings lead some users to belittle others.[2] Another thread is titled around the effects of the blackpill going mainstream on looks inflation.[6]

A further thread asks how far looks inflation would rise if lower-rated people were removed from the pool being compared, which treats the effect as a property of who is in the comparison group.[4] These are members' theories and are presented as such.

Contrast effects are a general perceptual principle: a stimulus is judged differently depending on what was seen just before or alongside it, and encyclopedic definitions use attractiveness judgments as an example, where a person appears more or less attractive depending on the comparison.[10] The halo effect, named by Edward Thorndike in his 1920 paper on rating errors, describes how one positive impression colours judgments of other traits, and the 1972 Dion, Berscheid and Walster study found that photographed people judged attractive were assumed to have more desirable personalities.[11]

These findings concern individual judgments, not a long-term drift in the standards of a community, and they have not been applied by researchers to the PSL scale. Forum posters use similar language informally, for instance when they describe an overconfidence halo created by inflated self-ratings.[2]

The term appears in rating and discussion threads as shorthand when comparing eras, when disputing a rating, or when arguing that a tier label no longer means what it once did.[1][7][8] A recurring counterpoint in the same threads is that a model-level or "pretty boy" face has broad appeal regardless of tier label.[1]

Posters who accept the idea draw practical conclusions: that grooming, skin and physique are a moving target, and that benchmarks should be real people rather than edited images.[2][3] Posters who dispute it argue that appeal to women, rather than a forum rating, is what counts.[1]

Mainstream coverage of looksmaxxing from outlets such as Vice, The Guardian and the BBC between 2018 and 2024 has focused on rating culture, bonesmashing and chin extensions, and later coverage in 2026 on influencers and drug use; none of the coverage summarised in the encyclopedia article addresses looksflation as a concept.[9] Critics of rating culture link it to body-image concerns, and some forum posters raise a similar worry about harsh peer rating.[9][2]
No studies found. Related, but separate, research covers contrast effects and the halo effect in judging attractiveness.[10][11]

timeline.event: Edward Thorndike publishes the paper that names the halo effect, an influence of one impression on other judgments.[11]
Dion, Berscheid and Walster report that people shown photos of attractive individuals credit them with more desirable traits.[11]
The term looksmaxxing emerges from online forums, with the PSL scale and tier labels as shared vocabulary.[9]
A looksmax.org poster dates a rise in tier boundaries to this period, when rating talk mainstreamed.[2]
Mainstream outlets including The Guardian and the BBC cover looksmaxxing and its rating culture.[9]

lore.intro: Looksflation is discussed in rating-scale and general discussion threads on looksmax.org, with a number of threads whose titles refer to looks inflation directly.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8]

claims.claim: "Bar to be chad is hyper-inflated" and keeps rising
claims.believers: Posters say constant exposure to edited, filtered images from a young age raises what people expect.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have measured drift in rating standards within looksmaxxing communities. Psychology describes contrast effects in individual attractiveness judgments.[10]

claims.claim: Generous self-ratings pushed tier boundaries up
claims.believers: One poster argues that users rating themselves high-tier raised boundaries and created an overconfidence halo.[2]
claims.experts: No published study has tested this. The halo effect is documented for how one impression colours other judgments.[11]

claims.claim: Older celebrities would be rated lower today
claims.believers: Members cite classic-film actors who were widely admired at the time but receive middling forum ratings now.[3]
claims.experts: No published study has compared historical and current rating standards on these scales.

claims.claim: Social media is the main driver
claims.believers: A dedicated thread and the posts above attribute the rise to filtered and edited images shown to young people.[5][3]
claims.experts: No published study has linked social media exposure to changes in PSL-style ratings.

claims.claim: Mainstreaming of the blackpill and rating culture accelerated it
claims.believers: Posters say that once rating talk spread beyond the early forums, more people rated themselves and others, shifting tier boundaries.[6][2]
claims.experts: Coverage of looksmaxxing records its spread but does not report any measurement of changing standards.[9]

claims.claim: A model-level face keeps broad appeal whatever the tier label
claims.believers: A poster argues that a prettyboy face earns appeal comparable to a Chad regardless of rating inflation.[1]
claims.experts: No published study has tested how forum tier labels relate to real-world appeal.
